analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals, nursing homes, and home care agencies to write and follow plans protecting staff from workplace violence.
analysis.headline: A bill requiring hospitals, nursing homes, and home health agencies to adopt workplace violence prevention plans drew 36 Senate cosponsors but never got a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Labor Department to write a workplace violence prevention standard for health care and social service employers. Hospitals, nursing homes, psychiatric facilities, home health agencies, and similar employers would have to create written prevention plans, assess risks, install safety measures like alarms and barriers, investigate incidents, train staff, and keep records of violent incidents. Employers who report violence would be protected from retaliation, and hospitals and nursing homes not already covered by workplace safety law would have to comply as a condition of receiving Medicare funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Health care and social service workers — nurses, aides, emergency responders, home health visitors, and social workers — would gain enforceable protection from violence on the job. The bill requires their participation in writing each facility's plan, mandates annual training and incident investigations, bars employers from retaliating against workers who report threats or attacks, and lets employees and their representatives inspect the incident records. Patients also benefit indirectly from calmer, safer facilities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nurses, aides, and social service workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires every covered employer — hospitals, nursing homes, psychiatric facilities, group homes, and home health and emergency services — to develop a written workplace violence prevention plan tailored to each facility, with the meaningful participation of direct care employees and their representatives.

Mandates concrete safety measures, not just paperwork: risk assessments informed by past incidents, engineering controls such as alarm systems, weapon detectors, access controls and physical barriers, and work practice controls including adequate staffing, security personnel, and de-escalation training.

Requires employers to investigate every violent incident, keep a detailed incident log for at least five years, submit annual reports to the Labor Department, and make those records available to employees and their unions; workers who report violence are protected from retaliation.

Gives the standard teeth by amending the Social Security Act so hospitals and skilled nursing facilities not otherwise covered by workplace safety law must comply with the standard as a condition of participating in Medicare.
Fast-tracks the rule: the Labor Department must issue an interim standard within one year, with a period (up to one year) of technical assistance to help employers comply before enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, nursing homes, psychiatric and residential treatment facilities, home health agencies, and staffing firms would bear the cost of written plans, security equipment and engineering controls, additional staff or security personnel where needed, annual training, and five years of incident recordkeeping. The Labor Department would bear the cost of writing and enforcing the standard. Those costs would largely be passed on through health care prices and government health programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and home care agencies

drawbacks.text: The bill bypasses the usual rulemaking guardrails: it exempts the interim standard from the Occupational Safety and Health Act's normal standard-setting procedures, the Paperwork Reduction Act, and executive order cost-benefit review, allowing only a 30-day public comment period. That speeds help to workers but limits scrutiny of the rule's cost and design.

Compliance is expensive for providers already operating on thin margins, especially nursing homes and rural hospitals: the bill contemplates spending on alarms, weapon detectors, access controls, security guards, and 'sufficient numbers of staff,' plus ongoing training, annual evaluations, and five-year recordkeeping.

The coverage line is not obvious: solo physician, dentist, and podiatrist offices are excluded, while a very broad set of other settings is included, and the Labor Department may add facilities it deems covered — leaving room for dispute about which employers must comply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is straightforward: real, enforceable protection for workers in settings where violence is a known occupational hazard, paid for through compliance spending by health care employers and ultimately through health prices and public programs. The design has genuine strengths — worker participation in plans, engineering controls, incident logs, and Medicare leverage — and a real weakness in bypassing normal cost-benefit review for the interim rule. On the whole the bill is a well-built worker safety mandate, not a badly designed one; the honest objection is its cost to underfunded providers, not its mechanics.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor issues the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on May 11, 2022, with 26 original cosponsors, all Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats.
It was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which was its first and only action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed.
Cosponsorship grew to 35 senators — 34 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents — but no Republican signed on.
The bill never left committee and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023; bills not passed by the end of a Congress must start over from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, nursing homes, and other covered health care employers came out ahead: they never faced a binding federal requirement to build violence prevention plans, install safety controls, or log and report violent incidents.

for.name: Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 26 original cosponsors.

against.name: Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: Hospital, nursing home, and home care industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory federal workplace violence prevention standards as costly regulatory mandates on providers.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 36 supporters — 34 of 48 Democrats and 1 of 2 independents — was a Democrat or Democratic-caucusing independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a floor vote where party splits would be recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have required written violence prevention plans, security equipment, staffing and training investments, and five years of incident logging and reporting across inpatient, outpatient, emergency, and psychiatric settings, with Medicare participation on the line for hospitals not otherwise covered by workplace safety law. Its interest in avoiding those costs runs against the workers the bill protects.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: Skilled nursing, hospice, memory care, and long-term care facilities are squarely covered, and the bill's reference to 'sufficient numbers of staff' points at an industry where understaffing is chronic. Compliance costs would land on operators already dependent on Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement.

industries.industry: Home health and social service agencies
industries.note: Field settings — home health care, home-based hospice, home-based social work — and emergency transport are covered services, so agencies would need plans and controls for workers who enter private homes and ride ambulances, where fixed engineering controls are hardest to deploy.

industries.industry: Health care staffing and temporary employment firms
industries.note: Contractors, subcontractors, temporary service firms, and employee leasing entities are explicitly covered employers, so staffing firms would share responsibility for prevention plans and training for the workers they place.
